ethics_check.report:

> In the familiarization phase of an auditory speech segmentation SL paradigm, participants are exposed to a speech stream without pauses or other (prosodic) cues for word boundaries.

> In addition, participants filled out a questionnaire about general musical ability and musical training experience (Gold-MSI: Bouwer et al., 2016; Müllensiefen et al., 2014).

> Participants were recruited through the participant database of the Institute for Language Sciences at Utrecht University, as well as through advertising both offline using flyers and online via social media.

> Participants were right-handed, native speakers of Dutch.

> Sensitivity analyses excluding these four participants did not alter the results and are additionally reported (section 3).

> These older participants were not included in van der Wulp et al. (2025), due to the age limit of 35 years that was preregistered for that project.

> Participants were compensated with a €20 gift card for their time.

> With respect to the rating task, participants were auditorily presented with a word or foil in each trial.

> The second post-learning task our participants performed was the TDT (Batterink, 2017; Batterink & Paller, 2017, 2019).

> Participants were presented (auditorily and visually) with a target syllable and subsequently heard a shortened version of the structured condition from the listening task, containing 16 words (4 words each repeated 4 times) corresponding to 48 syllables, and the same word not repeated in succession.

> Participants were instructed to press a button as quickly and accurately as possible upon hearing the target syllable.

> Furthermore, participants completed the Computerized Adaptive Beat Alignment Task (CA-BAT; Harrison & Müllensiefen, 2018b, 2018a).

> In this task, the participants were asked to compare auditorily presented rhythms and indicated how certain they were that these rhythms were the same or different.

> In addition, we administered the Speech-to-Speech Synchronization (SSS) task (Assaneo et al., 2019; Lizcano-Cortés et al., 2022) Participants were instructed to whisper 'tah' while listening to a syllable stream and to recall afterwards which syllables were presented.

> Participants were administered the forward Digit Span (Wechsler, 2008) as an indication of WM capacity.

> Furthermore, in our previous study including only neurotypical adults (van der Wulp et al., 2025), the results suggested that the stimuli we used -the same as in the current study -encompass less-frequently used syllables in the native language of our participants (Dutch) compared to the stimuli employed in earlier work (e.g., Batterink & Paller, 2017; Saffran, Aslin, et al., 1996).

> In addition, SSS data of three TR participants were excluded due to technical issues which made score calculation technically impossible.

> Each participant had between 50 and 70 epoch bundles, yielding more statistical power than the block analyses (section 3.2.1).

> We have additionally repeated this analysis while excluding the four participants with comorbid ADHD.

> Furthermore, removing the four participants with ADHD from the sample did also not alter these results either (see JASP supplement).

> Also, when we excluded the four participants with comorbid ADHD, or used the averaged ITCword as the dependent variable, the null model became the best model in all analyses (see JASP supplement).

> Participants completed a questionnaire including a Dutch translation of the Goldsmiths Musical Sophistication Index (Gold-MSI; Bouwer et al., 2016; Müllensiefen et al., 2014) measuring general musical ability.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 176 columns across 8 data files.
#### Issues Identified
7 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("TRDD_Rating.csv", "data_DD_JASP_R1.jasp", "data_DD_JASP_R1.jasp", "data_DD_JASP_R1.jasp", "data_DD_JASP_R1.jasp", "data_DD_JASP_R1.jasp", "data_DD_JASP_R1.jasp"), Column = c("(whole file)", "Condition", "Education", "Group", "INCL_ADHDsens", "gender", "ppID"), Issues = c("ℹ️ Space-separated .csv — This file is separated by spaces, not commas, so it reads as a sing...", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 143 values are missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 143 values are missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 143 values are missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 143 values are missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 143 values are missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 143 values are missing" )), row.names = c(NA, -7L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 8 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: In the familiarization phase of an auditory speech segmentation SL paradigm, participants are exposed to a speech stream without pauses or other (prosodic) cues for word boundaries.
In addition, participants filled out a questionnaire about general musical ability and musical training experience (Gold-MSI: Bouwer et al., 2016; Müllensiefen et al., 2014).

Participants were recruited through the participant database of the Institute for Language Sciences at Utrecht University, as well as through advertising both offline using flyers and online via social media.
Participants were right-handed, native speakers of Dutch.
Sensitivity analyses excluding these four participants did not alter the results and are additionally reported (section 3).
These older participants were not included in van der Wulp et al. (2025), due to the age limit of 35 years that was preregistered for that project.
Participants were compensated with a €20 gift card for their time.
With respect to the rating task, participants were auditorily presented with a word or foil in each trial.
The second post-learning task our participants performed was the TDT (Batterink, 2017; Batterink & Paller, 2017, 2019).

Participants were presented (auditorily and visually) with a target syllable and subsequently heard a shortened version of the structured condition from the listening task, containing 16 words (4 words each repeated 4 times) corresponding to 48 syllables, and the same word not repeated in succession.
Participants were instructed to press a button as quickly and accurately as possible upon hearing the target syllable.
Furthermore, participants completed the Computerized Adaptive Beat Alignment Task (CA-BAT; Harrison & Müllensiefen, 2018b, 2018a).
In this task, the participants were asked to compare auditorily presented rhythms and indicated how certain they were that these rhythms were the same or different.

In addition, we administered the Speech-to-Speech Synchronization (SSS) task (Assaneo et al., 2019; Lizcano-Cortés et al., 2022) Participants were instructed to whisper 'tah' while listening to a syllable stream and to recall afterwards which syllables were presented.
Participants were administered the forward Digit Span (Wechsler, 2008) as an indication of WM capacity.
The PPVT is a task where participants are presented with a word and four pictures in each trial.

Furthermore, in our previous study including only neurotypical adults (van der Wulp et al., 2025), the results suggested that the stimuli we used -the same as in the current study -encompass less-frequently used syllables in the native language of our participants (Dutch) compared to the stimuli employed in earlier work (e.g., Batterink & Paller, 2017; Saffran, Aslin, et al., 1996).
In addition, SSS data of three TR participants were excluded due to technical issues which made score calculation technically impossible.
Each participant had between 50 and 70 epoch bundles, yielding more statistical power than the block analyses (section 3.2.1).
We have additionally repeated this analysis while excluding the four participants with comorbid ADHD.
Furthermore, removing the four participants with ADHD from the sample did also not alter these results either (see JASP supplement).
Also, when we excluded the four participants with comorbid ADHD, or used the averaged ITCword as the dependent variable, the null model became the best model in all analyses (see JASP supplement).

Participants completed a questionnaire including a Dutch translation of the Goldsmiths Musical Sophistication Index (Gold-MSI; Bouwer et al., 2016; Müllensiefen et al., 2014) measuring general musical ability.

> one_split <- function(df) {
>   # randomly assign trials to halves, within ppID x pos
>   halves <- df %>%
>     filter(pos %in% c(1, 3)) %>%
>     distinct(ppID, trial, pos) %>%
>     group_by(ppID, pos) %>%
>     mutate(half = sample(rep(1:2, length.out = n()))) %>%
>     ungroup()
> 
>   scores <- df %>%
>     inner_join(halves, by = c("ppID", "trial", "pos")) %>%
>     group_by(ppID, half) %>%
>     summarise(m1 = mean(RT[pos == 1]),
>               m3 = mean(RT[pos == 3]),
>               score = (m1 - m3) / m1,
>               .groups = "drop") %>%
>     pivot_wider(id_cols = ppID, names_from = half,
>                 values_from = score, names_prefix = "h")
> 
>   r <- cor(scores$h1, scores$h2, use = "complete.obs")
>   2 * r / (1 + r)   # Spearman-Brown
> }

> one_split <- function(df) {
>   # randomly assign trials to halves, within ppID x pos
>   halves <- df %>%
>     filter(pos %in% c(1, 3)) %>%
>     distinct(ppID, trial, pos) %>%
>     group_by(ppID, pos) %>%
>     mutate(half = sample(rep(1:2, length.out = n()))) %>%
>     ungroup()
> 
>   scores <- df %>%
>     inner_join(halves, by = c("ppID", "trial", "pos")) %>%
>     group_by(ppID, half) %>%
>     summarise(m1 = mean(RT[pos == 1]),
>               m3 = mean(RT[pos == 3]),
>               score = (m1 - m3) / m1,
>               .groups = "drop") %>%
>     pivot_wider(id_cols = ppID, names_from = half,
>                 values_from = score, names_prefix = "h")
> 
>   r <- cor(scores$h1, scores$h2, use = "complete.obs")
>   2 * r / (1 + r)   # Spearman-Brown
> }

info.title: Neural evidence for intact statistical learning in Developmental Dyslexia in the absence of conclusive behavioral results: an individual differences approach to cognitive correlates

author.affiliation:
Institute for Language Sciences
								Utrecht University
								
									Utrecht
									the Netherlands

text.text: • Dyslexic and Typical Readers showed similar neural evidence of statistical learning.
• Behavioral SL performance was lower in dyslexic adults, but the difference was statistically inconclusive.
• Cognitive and rhythmic ability tasks related similarly to neural SL across groups.
• Findings stress individual differences over diagnostic group differences in SL.

Developmental Dyslexia (henceforth: DD) is defined as a specific learning disorder characterized by impaired reading and spelling despite normal intelligence and sensory abilities (American Psychiatric Association, 2022).
text.formatted: Developmental Dyslexia (henceforth: DD) is defined as a specific learning disorder characterized by impaired reading and spelling despite normal intelligence and sensory abilities <ref type="bibr">(American Psychiatric Association, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The prevalence of DD is approximately 7% of the population when DD is defined as having a standardized reading test score that is more than 1.5 SD below the age-appropriate average (Peterson & Pennington, 2015).
text.formatted: The prevalence of DD is approximately 7% of the population when DD is defined as having a standardized reading test score that is more than 1.5 SD below the age-appropriate average <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Peterson & Pennington, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The primary deficit reported for DD is poor grapheme-to-phoneme decoding, despite seemingly intact spoken language abilities.
However, auditory phoneme discrimination and phoneme awareness are also often reported to be impaired in individuals with DD.
Atypical neural entrainment responses to speech have been reported for DD as well (e.g., Goswami, 2011).
text.formatted: Atypical neural entrainment responses to speech have been reported for DD as well (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Goswami, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, adults with DD tend to have smaller vocabularies than their neurotypical peers and seem to underperform on reading comprehension (Ransby & Lee Swanson, 2003), both of which may be due to less print exposure (Suk, 2017).
text.formatted: Furthermore, adults with DD tend to have smaller vocabularies than their neurotypical peers and seem to underperform on reading comprehension <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">(Ransby & Lee Swanson, 2003)</ref>, both of which may be due to less print exposure <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">(Suk, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: A variety of explanatory accounts have linked DD to underlying neurocognitive impairments.

One such account states that individuals with DD are impaired in Statistical Learning (SL), which generally refers to the brain's implicit learning ability that makes use of statistical regularities to extract patterns in a variety of stimulus arrays (Gabay et al., 2015; Nicolson & Fawcett, 2011).
text.formatted: One such account states that individuals with DD are impaired in Statistical Learning (SL), which generally refers to the brain's implicit learning ability that makes use of statistical regularities to extract patterns in a variety of stimulus arrays <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Gabay et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Nicolson & Fawcett, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Learning to map graphemes to phonemes indeed entails a form of probabilistic learning, as one letter (such as the 'c') can map to multiple phonemes (e.g., 'cat' articulated as /kæt/, versus 'citrus' articulated as /ˈsɪtɹəs/ in English) or vice versa (e.g., /f/ being coded as "f" in fun, "ph" in phone, and "gh" in enough).

In previous research, SL ability in several domains was found to be related to reading outcomes in the general population (e.g., visual SL: Arciuli & Simpson, 2012; auditory SL: Spencer et al., 2015;  for a mixed-modality meta-analysis see: Lee et al., 2022).
text.formatted: In previous research, SL ability in several domains was found to be related to reading outcomes in the general population (e.g., visual SL: <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Arciuli & Simpson, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr">auditory SL: Spencer et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr"/> for a mixed-modality meta-analysis see: <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Lee et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: As SL is often hypothesized to be a domain-general learning mechanism (e.g., visual, auditory, tactile domains, as well as involving adjacent and non-adjacent pattern learning), researchers hypothesized that there may be a domain-general SL deficit underlying the learning difficulties in DD, and some evidence for this domaingeneral SL deficit-hypothesis was indeed obtained (Lee et al., 2022).
text.formatted: As SL is often hypothesized to be a domain-general learning mechanism (e.g., visual, auditory, tactile domains, as well as involving adjacent and non-adjacent pattern learning), researchers hypothesized that there may be a domain-general SL deficit underlying the learning difficulties in DD, and some evidence for this domaingeneral SL deficit-hypothesis was indeed obtained <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Lee et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, an increasing body of literature suggests that SL is not a domain-general capacity, but instead consists of multiple components, where different tasks used to assess SL tap into different components (Arciuli, 2017; Singh & Conway, 2021; Siegelman, Bogaerts, Christiansen, et al., 2017; Siegelman & Frost, 2015).
text.formatted: However, an increasing body of literature suggests that SL is not a domain-general capacity, but instead consists of multiple components, where different tasks used to assess SL tap into different components <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Arciuli, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">Singh & Conway, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">Siegelman, Bogaerts, Christiansen, et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">Siegelman & Frost, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, within-individual differences in performance between tasks measuring SL online or post-exposure have also been found (Lukics & Lukács, 2021; Lukács et al., 2026; Siegelman & Frost, 2015).
text.formatted: Furthermore, within-individual differences in performance between tasks measuring SL online or post-exposure have also been found <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Lukics & Lukács, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Lukács et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">Siegelman & Frost, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: For the purposes of the current study investigating SL in DD, we focus on SL for speech segmentation (Saffran, Aslin, et al., 1996; Saffran, Newport, et al., 1996), and include both online neural entrainment and offline post-exposure tests of SL.
text.formatted: For the purposes of the current study investigating SL in DD, we focus on SL for speech segmentation <ref type="bibr">(Saffran, Aslin, et al., 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Saffran, Newport, et al., 1996)</ref>, and include both online neural entrainment and offline post-exposure tests of SL.

text.text: Studies investigating neurodevelopmental disorders have mostly focused on group comparisons, classifying the diagnosis-based group as 'one kind of individual.'
What is often overlooked in these studies is individual variability.

In line with previous accounts (Arciuli, 2017; Arciuli & Conway, 2018; Bogaerts et al., 2022; Erickson & Thiessen, 2015; Lukács et al., 2026; Siegelman, 2020; Siegelman & Frost, 2015), we hypothesize that an individual's SL ability can be influenced by (interactions between) multiple cognitive factors.
text.formatted: In line with previous accounts <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Arciuli, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Arciuli & Conway, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Bogaerts et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Erickson & Thiessen, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Lukács et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">Siegelman, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">Siegelman & Frost, 2015)</ref>, we hypothesize that an individual's SL ability can be influenced by (interactions between) multiple cognitive factors.

text.text: These factors can either facilitate or impair SL, which could explain at least some of the individual variability on SL task performance across groups with and without language-related impairments (cf., Arciuli & Conway, 2018; Lukács et al., 2026).
text.formatted: These factors can either facilitate or impair SL, which could explain at least some of the individual variability on SL task performance across groups with and without language-related impairments (cf., <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Arciuli & Conway, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Lukács et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Candidate cognitive factors investigated in the current study are Working Memory (WM) and musical Rhythmic Ability (RA).
First, we will review the literature on SL for speech segmentation.
There are indications that SL plays a role in language acquisition prior to the acquisition of literacy skills.
For example, SL supports speech segmentation, which is necessary for vocabulary acquisition.
Clear and consistent acoustic cues indicating word boundaries are sparse in spoken languages.
Therefore, speech segmentation poses a challenge to language learners.

SL is hypothesized to underpin this process because it allows learners to use statistical regularities, or Transitional Probabilities (TPs), between adjacent syllables to estimate the chance of a word boundary in continuous speech.
TP of 𝑌|𝑋 = 𝑓𝑟𝑒𝑞𝑢𝑒𝑛𝑐𝑦 𝑜𝑓 𝑋𝑌 𝑓𝑟𝑒𝑞𝑢𝑒𝑛𝑐𝑦 𝑜𝑓 𝑋 TPs within words are higher than TPs between words, and the learner can thus assume a word boundary when a 'dip' in TPs is detected (Saffran, 2003).
text.formatted: TP of 𝑌|𝑋 = 𝑓𝑟𝑒𝑞𝑢𝑒𝑛𝑐𝑦 𝑜𝑓 𝑋𝑌 𝑓𝑟𝑒𝑞𝑢𝑒𝑛𝑐𝑦 𝑜𝑓 𝑋 TPs within words are higher than TPs between words, and the learner can thus assume a word boundary when a 'dip' in TPs is detected <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">(Saffran, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Speech segmentation based on TPs has been extensively studied in laboratory settings with both infants (Choi et al., 2020; Saffran, Aslin, et al., 1996; Singh et al., 2012, i.a.) and adults (e.g., Batterink & Paller, 2017; Saffran, Newport, et al., 1996; Zhang et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Speech segmentation based on TPs has been extensively studied in laboratory settings with both infants <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Choi et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Saffran, Aslin, et al., 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Singh et al., 2012, i.a.)</ref> and adults (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Batterink & Paller, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Saffran, Newport, et al., 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">Zhang et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Its role in language acquisition is indicated by reported associations between individual differences in SL and language outcomes, including reading ability (e.g., Lee et al., 2022; Spencer et al., 2015) and vocabulary size (Erickson & Thiessen, 2015; Siegelman, 2020; Singh et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Its role in language acquisition is indicated by reported associations between individual differences in SL and language outcomes, including reading ability (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Lee et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">Spencer et al., 2015)</ref> and vocabulary size <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Erickson & Thiessen, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">Siegelman, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">Singh et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: SL is usually investigated in laboratory settings including a familiarization and test phase.
In the familiarization phase of an auditory speech segmentation SL paradigm, participants are exposed to a speech stream without pauses or other (prosodic) cues for word boundaries.
The speech stream contains multi-syllabic 'words,' with TPs within words being 1.0, whereas TPs between words are lower (e.g., 0.33 in the case of a speech stream comprising four words).
In the test phase, participants behaviorally judge their familiarity with presented words and foils, usually consisting of part-words that span a word boundary.
In some cases, non-word foils are also included, consisting of syllable strings never presented consecutively in the familiarization phase.

Accuracy of judgement (i.e., words being judged as more familiar than foils) is then taken as an indication of SL ability (e.g., Batterink & Paller, 2017; van der Wulp et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Accuracy of judgement (i.e., words being judged as more familiar than foils) is then taken as an indication of SL ability (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Batterink & Paller, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b112">van der Wulp et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">Zhang et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: However, such post-hoc familiarity rating tasks have been criticized in the literature for relying on meta-cognitive decision-making (Bogaerts et al., 2022) and insufficient psychometric reliability to measure SL ability on an individual level (for visual SL : Siegelman et al., 2017; auditory SL: 2018, see also Siegelman, Bogaerts, Christiansen, et al., 2017).
text.formatted: However, such post-hoc familiarity rating tasks have been criticized in the literature for relying on meta-cognitive decision-making <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Bogaerts et al., 2022)</ref> and insufficient psychometric reliability to measure SL ability on an individual level (for visual SL <ref type="bibr">: Siegelman et al., 2017</ref>; auditory SL: 2018, see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">Siegelman, Bogaerts, Christiansen, et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, 'target detection' tasks measuring Reaction Times (RTs) to specific 'target' syllables in the speech stream are also employed as post-exposure measurements assessing implicit memory of the words (Batterink & Paller, 2017; 2019).
text.formatted: In addition, 'target detection' tasks measuring Reaction Times (RTs) to specific 'target' syllables in the speech stream are also employed as post-exposure measurements assessing implicit memory of the words <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Batterink & Paller, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">2019)</ref>.

text.text: If successful SL occurred during familiarization, faster RTs are expected to target syllables in word-final positions, compared to word-initial syllables.
This difference in RTs per syllable position is referred to as the RT facilitation effect (Batterink & Paller, 2017; 2019; van der Wulp et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This difference in RTs per syllable position is referred to as the RT facilitation effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Batterink & Paller, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b112">van der Wulp et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: While behavioral post-exposure tasks may assess both explicit and implicit memory traces of the words acquired through SL, these tasks do not measure the process of identifying TPs during the familiarization phase.

Using electroencephalography (EEG), the process of SL in the brain during familiarization can be measured (e.g., Batterink & Paller, 2017; Choi et al., 2020; Moreau et al., 2022; van der Wulp et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Using electroencephalography (EEG), the process of SL in the brain during familiarization can be measured (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Batterink & Paller, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Choi et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Moreau et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b112">van der Wulp et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">Zhang et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The neural measurement indicates the amount of brain activity phase-locked or entrained to the frequency of the words and syllables.
When syllable lengths are equated -for example at 300 ms -the corresponding syllable presentation frequency is 3.3 Hz.
When words are three syllables long (as suggested by the TP structure), the word length is 900 ms and the corresponding word frequency is 1.1 Hz.
Such syllable and word frequencies were previously found to emerge in the oscillatory activity of the brain during SL (e.g., Batterink & Paller, 2017).
text.formatted: Such syllable and word frequencies were previously found to emerge in the oscillatory activity of the brain during SL (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Batterink & Paller, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: This is operationalized by computing the Inter-Trial Coherence (ITC) for the frequencies of interest.
The ITC ranges from 0 (no phase-locking at all to a given frequency) to 1 (perfectly phase-locked neural activity to a given frequency).

An increasing ITC to the frequency of presented multi-syllabic words is taken to reflect SL, whereas neural entrainment to the syllable frequency indicates auditory processing of the syllabic units in the acoustic signal.

A control condition then consists of randomly concatenated syllables, where neural entrainment to multisyllabic units is not expected based on the TP structure of the speech stream (Batterink & Paller, 2017; van der Wulp et al., 2025).
text.formatted: A control condition then consists of randomly concatenated syllables, where neural entrainment to multisyllabic units is not expected based on the TP structure of the speech stream <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Batterink & Paller, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b112">van der Wulp et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Is there evidence for a statistical learning deficit in Developmental Dyslexia?
Many studies report individual variability in SL in the general population (see Bogaerts et al., 2022 for review).
text.formatted: Many studies report individual variability in SL in the general population (see <ref type="bibr">Bogaerts et al.,</ref> 2022 for review).

text.text: As SL relates to language abilities (e.g., Siegelman, 2020; Lukács et al., 2026), behavioral studies comparing SL in groups with language-related impairments, including DD, have been frequently conducted.
text.formatted: As SL relates to language abilities (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">Siegelman, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Lukács et al., 2026)</ref>, behavioral studies comparing SL in groups with language-related impairments, including DD, have been frequently conducted.

text.text: The current evidence for a SL deficit in DD is mixed: some studies did find evidence in favor of a SL deficit in dyslexia across multiple domains (e.g., Gabay et al., 2015; Kerkhoff et al., 2013; Kligler & Gabay, 2023; Lum et al., 2013; Ozernov-Palchik et al., 2023; Vandermosten et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2021; see Lee et al., 2022 for meta-analysis) while others reported no difference between DD and control groups (e.g., Daikoku et al., 2023; Schmalz et al., 2017; van Witteloostuijn et al., 2019).
text.formatted: The current evidence for a SL deficit in DD is mixed: some studies did find evidence in favor of a SL deficit in dyslexia across multiple domains (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Gabay et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Kerkhoff et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Kligler & Gabay, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Lum et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Ozernov-Palchik et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b116">Vandermosten et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">Zhang et al., 2021</ref>; see <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Lee et al., 2022</ref> for meta-analysis) while others reported no difference between DD and control groups (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Daikoku et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">Schmalz et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b115">van Witteloostuijn et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: For an extensive review of literature on DD and SL in both children and adults, we refer the interested reader to Singh and Conway (2021).
text.formatted: For an extensive review of literature on DD and SL in both children and adults, we refer the interested reader to <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">Singh and Conway (2021)</ref>.

text.text: Of particular interest to the current study focusing on SL for speech segmentation is an EEG experiment recently conducted by Zhang and colleagues (2021).
text.formatted: Of particular interest to the current study focusing on SL for speech segmentation is an EEG experiment recently conducted by <ref type="bibr">Zhang and colleagues (2021)</ref>.

text.text: For the first time in a population with DD, they employed EEG measurements of neural entrainment (as detailed in section 1.1.1 above) to investigate SL in a speech segmentation experiment.

The authors compared participants with DD to a Typical Reader (TR) group in a structured language condition (containing words) and a random language condition (consisting of randomly ordered syllables).
In addition, they compared the groups on a behavioral task measuring their memory outcomes of learning in the structured language condition.
On the behavioral level, Zhang et al. (2021) report no significant difference between the groups.
text.formatted: On the behavioral level, <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">Zhang et al. (2021)</ref> report no significant difference between the groups.

text.text: With regard to the neural data, the authors reported no significant differences between the groups for syllable-rate neural tracking in both conditions.
On the other hand, Zhang et al. (2021) did report a significant difference in the neural tracking of the words in the structured language condition between the TR and DD groups.
text.formatted: On the other hand, <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">Zhang et al. (2021)</ref> did report a significant difference in the neural tracking of the words in the structured language condition between the TR and DD groups.

text.text: The DD group showed less neural tracking of the word frequency than the TR group averaged over the entire exposure period.
Furthermore, word-level entrainment increased over time for both groups in the structured language condition, but more slowly in the DD group than in the TR group.

A repeated-measures ANOVA with group (TR/DD), language condition (structured/random), and block (time) as predictors showed a trend towards a quadratic three-way interaction (Zhang et al., 2021, p. 5).

text.text: Both groups did not show increasing word-level entrainment in the random control condition, in line with earlier research (Batterink & Paller, 2017). Zhang et al. (2021) argue that the lack of a significant interaction is probably due to a limited sample size (N = 18 per group) and therefore limited statistical power.

text.text: As mentioned above, we hypothesize that individual differences in SL ability can be influenced by multiple cognitive factors either facilitating or impairing SL.
We hypothesize that these factors could explain some of the individual variability in SL task performance across groups with and without language-related impairments.

Such individual differences have mainly been studied in the typical population, whereas research investigating SL in groups with language impairments usually relies on group comparisons between the diagnostic and control groups.
However, it is highly likely that there is individual variability within both populations.

In the current study, we investigate Working Memory and Rhythmic Ability as candidate cognitive factors impacting SL in both the neurotypical population as well as the population diagnosed with DD, for reasons detailed below.
Working Memory (WM) has frequently been theorized to subserve SL (e.g., Arciuli, 2017; Misyak & Christiansen, 2012; Siegelman & Frost, 2015).
text.formatted: Working Memory (WM) has frequently been theorized to subserve SL (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Arciuli, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Misyak & Christiansen, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">Siegelman & Frost, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Regarding SL for speech segmentation, the learner needs to keep the (syllabic) units in short-term memory, maintaining them in a phonological rehearsal mechanism (Rodríguez-Fornells et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Regarding SL for speech segmentation, the learner needs to keep the (syllabic) units in short-term memory, maintaining them in a phonological rehearsal mechanism <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Rodríguez-Fornells et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Simultaneously, the SL mechanism identifies TPs between the syllabic items in the input.
When a lower TP indicates a word boundary, the syllables need to be transferred from short-term memory to the long-term memory as one word-like phonological unit.

Phonological WM impairments have been widely reported for DD at the group level, and seem to persist from childhood (Alt et al., 2022; Gray et al., 2019) into adulthood (Gabay et al., 2015; Smith-Spark & Fisk, 2007).
text.formatted: Phonological WM impairments have been widely reported for DD at the group level, and seem to persist from childhood <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Alt et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Gray et al., 2019)</ref> into adulthood <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Gabay et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">Smith-Spark & Fisk, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: However, individual variability within groups diagnosed with DD was found regarding WM capacity.
For instance, Gray et al. (2019) divided their sample of second graders (including those diagnosed with DD) into WM profiles from low to high task performance.
text.formatted: For instance, <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Gray et al. (2019)</ref> divided their sample of second graders (including those diagnosed with DD) into WM profiles from low to high task performance.

text.text: They found that children with DD were present in each profile, including the lowest and highest ones.
This indicates that WM is not universally impaired in DD, but that large individual differences regarding WM are present in the population diagnosed with DD.

To date, attempts to investigate relationships between individual differences in WM and SL in neurotypical populations yielded inconclusive results (e.g., Arciuli & Simpson, 2012; Misyak & Christiansen, 2012; Siegelman & Frost, 2015; van der Wulp et al., 2025).
text.formatted: To date, attempts to investigate relationships between individual differences in WM and SL in neurotypical populations yielded inconclusive results (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Arciuli & Simpson, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Misyak & Christiansen, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">Siegelman & Frost, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b112">van der Wulp et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This may be due to sample characteristics of most publications.
The aforementioned and related studies investigating WM contributions to SL have only included samples from the neurotypical population.
This can result in limited variance in both WM and SL scores.

Including wider (non-neurotypical) samples with more variation in SL and WM scores might reveal relationships between cognitive factors (such as WM) and SL which are not attested when these samples are excluded.

In a previous study (van der Wulp et al., 2025), we proposed that individual differences in SL for speech segmentation may at least partially be explained by individual differences in musical Rhythmic Ability (RA).
text.formatted: In a previous study <ref type="bibr" target="#b112">(van der Wulp et al., 2025)</ref>, we proposed that individual differences in SL for speech segmentation may at least partially be explained by individual differences in musical Rhythmic Ability (RA).

text.text: Here, RA is defined as an individual's ability to perceive the beat and recognize the meter in a rhythmic auditory signal, with corresponding neural or behavioral rhythmic synchronization to these external (musical) rhythms.

Our hypothesis is based on previous literature establishing correlations between RA and language development, as well as a neurocognitive overlap in mechanisms that underly both SL and RA in the brain.
First, both language and musical rhythm are hierarchically organized.
In rhythms, beats are at the level of sensory perception, from which a higher-level meter can be deduced: usually defined as an alternating pattern of strong and weak beats (Daikoku & Goswami, 2022).
text.formatted: In rhythms, beats are at the level of sensory perception, from which a higher-level meter can be deduced: usually defined as an alternating pattern of strong and weak beats <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Daikoku & Goswami, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly in language, syllables are at the level of sensory perception and are concatenated to form words.

RA has further been shown to predict language development in recent large-scale literature reviews (Fiveash et al., 2021; Ladányi et al., 2020), where atypical RA is correspondingly indicated as a risk factor for atypical language development, including DD.
text.formatted: RA has further been shown to predict language development in recent large-scale literature reviews <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Fiveash et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Ladányi et al., 2020)</ref>, where atypical RA is correspondingly indicated as a risk factor for atypical language development, including DD.

text.text: Second, there is evidence for shared neural mechanisms involved in processing musical rhythm and language.
Primary among these is the dorsal auditory processing stream (Hickok & Poeppel, 2007; Cannon & Patel, 2021).
text.formatted: Primary among these is the dorsal auditory processing stream <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Hickok & Poeppel, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Cannon & Patel, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This auditory dorsal pathway maps sensory representations from the auditory cortex onto motor representations in the motor cortex.

It is thought to underly spoken language acquisition (Hickok & Poeppel, 2007) and hypothesized to be a neural substrate of speech segmentation through SL (François et al., 2012; Rodríguez-Fornells et al., 2009).
text.formatted: It is thought to underly spoken language acquisition <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Hickok & Poeppel, 2007)</ref> and hypothesized to be a neural substrate of speech segmentation through SL <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(François et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Rodríguez-Fornells et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, in work by Assaneo and colleagues (2019), the white matter integrity of a tract that is part of the dorsal stream was found to be higher in adult participants who spontaneously synchronized their overt speech to the rhythm of an auditorily presented syllable sequence.
text.formatted: Furthermore, in work by <ref type="bibr">Assaneo and colleagues (2019)</ref>, the white matter integrity of a tract that is part of the dorsal stream was found to be higher in adult participants who spontaneously synchronized their overt speech to the rhythm of an auditorily presented syllable sequence.

text.text: These 'high synchronizers' further outperformed 'low synchronizers' in a behavioral SL speech segmentation task.
In addition, high synchronizers showed more neural entrainment to syllables while listening to speech.

Several studies indicated that RA correlates with linguistic abilities including reading (e.g., Bekius et al., 2016; Flaugnacco et al., 2014; Huss et al., 2011; Zuk et al., 2017; see Fiveash et al., 2021 and Ladányi et al., 2020 for reviews).
text.formatted: Several studies indicated that RA correlates with linguistic abilities including reading (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Bekius et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Flaugnacco et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Huss et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">Zuk et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">see Fiveash et al., 2021 and</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Ladányi et al., 2020</ref> for reviews).

text.text: Specifically, a large body of literature reports evidence for a rhythmic impairment in DD on both the behavioral (e.g., Bégel et al., 2022; Boll-Avetisyan et al., 2020; Caccia & Lorusso, 2021; Flaugnacco et al., 2014; Huss et al., 2011) and neural level (e.g., Chang et al., 2021; Colling et al., 2017; Peter et al., 2023; Power et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Specifically, a large body of literature reports evidence for a rhythmic impairment in DD on both the behavioral (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Bégel et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Boll-Avetisyan et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Caccia & Lorusso, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Flaugnacco et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Huss et al., 2011)</ref> and neural level (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Chang et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Colling et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Peter et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Power et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: These findings are in line with frameworks positing that individuals with DD show inefficient neural entrainment to auditory rhythmic stimuli such as speech and music (e.g., PRISM : Fiveash et al., 2021; Temporal Sampling Framework: Goswami, 2011; Atypical Rhythm Risk Hypothesis: Ladányi et al., 2020).
text.formatted: These findings are in line with frameworks positing that individuals with DD show inefficient neural entrainment to auditory rhythmic stimuli such as speech and music (e.g., PRISM <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">: Fiveash et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Temporal Sampling Framework: Goswami, 2011</ref>; Atypical Rhythm Risk Hypothesis: <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Ladányi et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Inefficient entrainment occurs when the neural oscillations of an individual do not reset their phase in such a way that the input arrives at the highest excitability state of the oscillation (see Figure 1; cf., Peelle & Davis, 2012).
text.formatted: Inefficient entrainment occurs when the neural oscillations of an individual do not reset their phase in such a way that the input arrives at the highest excitability state of the oscillation (see Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>; cf., <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Peelle & Davis, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: This inefficient neural entrainment would then affect both musical rhythm processing and phonological processing (Giraud & Poeppel, 2012; Goswami, 2011; Ladányi et al., 2020).
text.formatted: This inefficient neural entrainment would then affect both musical rhythm processing and phonological processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Giraud & Poeppel, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Goswami, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Ladányi et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This hypothesis is supported by a number of studies, specifically regarding entrainment to lowfrequency rhythmic input (delta/theta band) such as speech (e.g., the frequency of syllables/words) and music (Colling et al., 2017; Di Liberto et al., 2018; Fiveash et al., 2021 Fiveash et al., , 2021;; Hämäläinen et al., 2012; Ladányi et al., 2020; Mandke et al., 2022; Peter et al., 2023).

text.text: These findings have been taken to indicate atypical auditory dorsal stream functioning in people with DD.

Indeed, previous research found significant positive correlations between phonological processing, reading skills, and structural integrity in the auditory dorsal pathway in DD (Sihvonen et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Indeed, previous research found significant positive correlations between phonological processing, reading skills, and structural integrity in the auditory dorsal pathway in DD <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">(Sihvonen et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, musicians with DD are reported to benefit in their phonological processing ability from their musical training experience (e.g., Bishop-Liebler et al., 2014; Zuk et al., 2017), suggesting that musical training can improve some of the auditory processing impairments reported for DD.

text.text: We investigated individual differences in Statistical Learning (SL) for speech segmentation by additionally measuring Working Memory (WM) and Rhythmic Ability (RA) in samples of Developmental Dyslexia (DD) and Typical Readers (TR).
We investigated whether WM and/or RA are predictors for individual differences in SL in both these populations.
We hypothesized that if a relationship between WM/RA and SL is attested in the TR group, it would also be present in individuals diagnosed with DD.
Individual variability in DD with regard to WM/RA could then contribute to an explanation for the mixed results obtained in research on a possible SL deficit in DD.
In previous studies investigating SL in DD, RA was to our knowledge not yet investigated as a factor contributing to individual differences in this population and the broader population as a whole.

Specifically, we investigated: (1) Whether adults with DD show poorer SL ability, both behaviorally and neurally, compared to typical readers; (2) Whether adults with DD show weaker RA, phonological WM capacity, and vocabulary size, compared to typical readers; (3) Whether interindividual variations in RA, WM and vocabulary are similarly related to individual differences in SL abilities in individuals with DD compared to typical readers.

We predicted that the DD group would show less neural entrainment to the word frequency during SL, and/or a slower learning trajectory in their EEG responses during exposure to the structured language condition (as in Zhang et al., 2021, section 1.2).
Furthermore, we explored if there were behavioral differences in SL ability between the groups on a familiarity rating task and target detection task (cf. section 1.1.1).
We further predicted that the DD group would on average perform more poorly on tasks measuring RA and WM compared to the TR group, but we expected individual variability within both groups.
We tested RA using three tasks (CA-BAT:
Harrison & Müllensiefen, 2018b, 2018a; PROMS: Zentner & Strauss, 2017; SSS task: Assaneo et al., 2019; see section 2.3.3).
text.formatted: Harrison & Müllensiefen, 2018b, 2018a; PROMS: Zentner & Strauss, 2017; SSS task: Assaneo et al., 2019; see section <ref type="formula">2.3.3</ref>).

text.text: In addition, participants filled out a questionnaire about general musical ability and musical training experience (Gold-MSI: Bouwer et al., 2016; Müllensiefen et al., 2014).
text.formatted: In addition, participants filled out a questionnaire about general musical ability and musical training experience (Gold-MSI: <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Bouwer et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Müllensiefen et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: In order to investigate phonological WM capacity, we administered the forward Digit Span (Wechsler, 2008).
text.formatted: In order to investigate phonological WM capacity, we administered the forward Digit Span <ref type="bibr" target="#b117">(Wechsler, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: We predicted that RA/WM and SL would show a positive relation in both DD and TR groups, and that these relations would be similar in both groups.
If this is the case, we would contribute to explaining the mixed results obtained in previous studies on whether there is a SL deficit in DD.
Perhaps other factors such as WM/RA could explain individual differences in SL on a more continuous scale, instead of group distinctions based on diagnoses.

Finally, we administered a vocabulary test (Dunn & Dunn, 1998; Schlichting, 2005) to explore whether vocabulary size differs between the groups and to investigate if vocabulary size and SL also correlate positively in adults, as this was previously attested in children (e.g., Singh et al., 2012).

text.text: We collected data from a total of 143 participants.

Participants were recruited through the participant database of the Institute for Language Sciences at Utrecht University, as well as through advertising both offline using flyers and online via social media.
Participants were right-handed, native speakers of Dutch.
They were not invited to participate if they reported having an autism spectrum disorder, a history of hearing impairments or tinnitus, or neurological impairments.

Participants indicated whether they had been diagnosed with DD by a qualified professional with a yes/no question in a questionnaire and, if so, when they were diagnosed (during primary school, in high school, or after high school).

We did not conduct additional tests to verify the presence/absence or severity of DD, because the experiment session would then become too long and strenuous for the participants (the session took approximately two hours).
Twenty-five participants (19 F; 6 M) in our sample reported that they were diagnosed with DD by a qualified professional and formed the DD group.
Of these 25 participants, 13 (52%) indicated to have received their diagnosis during primary school, 11 (44%) during high school, and one (4%) after high school.
Their ages ranged from 19 to 43 years old (M = 25.04, SD = 5.46).
For a related project, we were simultaneously investigating Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD; van der Wulp et al., 2026a).
text.formatted: For a related project, we were simultaneously investigating Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD; van der <ref type="bibr">Wulp et al., 2026a)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, we did not exclude participants with comorbid DD and ADHD.
This was the case for N = 4 participants in the DD group.
Sensitivity analyses excluding these four participants did not alter the results and are additionally reported (section 3).

For the block-wise EEG analyses (see section 2.5.2), we combined the data from our DD group with the neural data (ITCword and ITCsyllable values) from the 18 participants in the DD group (12 F; 6 M; Mage = 23.9, SD = 4.00) of Zhang et al. (2021; 2025), to increase statistical power (Ntotal DD group = 43).

Participants were compensated with a €20 gift card for their time.
The stimuli consisted of syllables that were combined into tri-syllabic pseudowords (from now on referred to as 'words') that adhered to Dutch phonotactics.
The syllable inventory consisted of 12 syllables, from which four words were formed for the structured language condition: /suχita, tobamø, sytøbo, χøbyti/.
In this condition, the transitional probabilities of neighboring syllables were 1.0 within a word and 0.33 between words.
The word order was pseudorandomized, such that the same word did not repeat consecutively.
We also created a corresponding random language condition.
In this condition, a different set of 12 syllables was concatenated in a pseudorandom order, under the constraint that the same syllable could not consecutively repeat.
This yielded a transitional probability of 0.09 throughout the random language condition.
The syllables used in this condition were: /da, pø, nu, dø, χo, py, ro, dy, sa, χy, ri, sø/.
More details on the methodology used to create these stimuli are described in van der Wulp et al. (2022).

text.text: The stimulus lists were converted to concatenated speech without pauses using MBROLA diphone synthesis (male Dutch voice nl2, at a monotone F0 of 100 Hz; Dutoit et al., 1996).

Thus, this yielded a syllable frequency of 3.3 Hz and a word or triplet frequency of 1.1 Hz (see Figure 2).

text.text: We generated coarticulated speech streams of 13.5 minutes per condition in total, divided over three blocks of 4.5 minutes.
Each block was made up of 900 syllables (300 words).
We used GoldWave (GoldWave Inc., 2022) to add a linear fade-in and fade-out of 1.5 seconds at the beginning and end of each block, to avoid a segmentation cue at the beginning of the stream.
Stimuli were presented with Presentation (http://www.neurobs.com/).

text.text: Detailed descriptions of the procedure are provided in the following sections.
Participants first performed the listening task in the structured language condition.
After this, two behavioral tests for SL (rating task and target detection task) were administered, followed by another iteration of the listening task in the random language condition.
The listening task was divided into three blocks of 4.5 minutes per condition, yielding 13.5 minutes per condition and 27 minutes in total for both conditions.
Participants took short self-timed breaks between blocks.
During the listening task, neural responses were measured using electroencephalography (EEG; see section 2.4.1).

Following the structured language condition of the listening task, participants performed two tasks to assess their explicit and implicit knowledge of the words: a familiarity rating task and a reaction-time based Target Detection Task (TDT).
With respect to the rating task, participants were auditorily presented with a word or foil in each trial.
The foils could be of two kinds: one being a part-word spanning a word boundary from the stream, or a non-word made up of syllables from the stream but recombined in an order that never appeared.
There were 16 trials consisting of the four words from the listening task, all eight possible part-words and four non-words.
On each trial, participants rated on a four-point scale how familiar the word sounded to them (scale: unfamiliar -fairly unfamiliar -fairly familiar -familiar).
The second post-learning task our participants performed was the TDT (Batterink, 2017; Batterink & Paller, 2017 , 2019).
text.formatted: The second post-learning task our participants performed was the TDT <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Batterink, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Batterink & Paller, 2017</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Participants were presented (auditorily and visually) with a target syllable and subsequently heard a shortened version of the structured condition from the listening task, containing 16 words (4 words each repeated 4 times) corresponding to 48 syllables, and the same word not repeated in succession.
Participants were instructed to press a button as quickly and accurately as possible upon hearing the target syllable.
There were three speech streams per target syllable, with the target occurring four times per stream, resulting in 36 speech streams and 144 targets for this task.

>Data preparation
text.formatted: <head n="2.4." >Data preparation</head>

text.text: During the listening task, EEG was recorded at a sampling rate of 512 Hz using 64 Ag/AgCltipped electrodes attached to an electrode headcap using the 10/20 system.
Recordings were made with the Active-Two system (Biosemi, Amsterdam, The Netherlands).
Additional electrodes were placed on the left and right mastoid, above and below the left eye, and at the outer canthi of both eyes.
Scalp signals were recorded relative to the Common Mode Sense (CMS) active electrode and re-referenced during data analysis to the average of the mastoid electrodes.
Electrode offset of each channel compared to the reference electrode CMS was accepted below 20 mV.
If the impedance of a channel was higher than this, it was labeled as a bad channel during data collection to be interpolated during data analysis.
The EEG data was analyzed in MATLAB (The MathWorks Inc., 2019) using EEGLAB (Delorme & Makeig, 2004) and the ERPLAB open-source toolbox (Lopez-Calderon & Luck, 2014).
text.formatted: The EEG data was analyzed in MATLAB (The MathWorks Inc., 2019) using EEGLAB <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Delorme & Makeig, 2004)</ref> and the ERPLAB open-source toolbox <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Lopez-Calderon & Luck, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: The data was bandpass filtered from 0.1 to 30 Hz 2 and 50 Hz notch filtered offline.

Bad channels identified upon visual inspection of the data or during data collection were interpolated (mean N of interpolated channels TR group structured = 5.06, random = 6.46; DD group structured = 5.32, random = 7.48).
Data sections comprising large artifacts were also identified through visual inspection and manually rejected using the EEGLAB plugin VisEd (Desjardins et al., 2019).

text.text: A channel was labeled as bad during the analysis if it was labeled as such during data collection due to high impedance, or if it showed frequent noise or drifts upon visual inspection of the data.
Following previous work (Batterink & Paller, 2017; van der Wulp et al., 2025 van der Wulp et al., , 2026a van der Wulp et al., , 2026b)), eye movement artifacts were retained.

text.text: Eye movements were not time-locked to stimulus onsets and have a broad power spectrum that was found to leave the narrow-band neural oscillations unaffected (Srinivasan & Petrovic, 2006).

text.text: We time-locked the data to the onsets of the tri-syllabic words and divided the data into non-overlapping epochs of 10.8 seconds, corresponding to the duration of 12 trisyllabic words (36 syllables).
We then quantified phase-locking to the word (1.1 Hz) and syllable (3.3 Hz) frequencies using the Inter-Trial Coherence (ITC), which ranges from 0 to 1.
An ITC of 1 indicates perfect phase-locked neural activity to a given frequency, and 0 indicates no phaselocking at all to that frequency.

The ITC was calculated after a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) for each epoch across frequency bins of interest: between 0.6 to 5 Hz, with a bin width of 0.09 2 Eighteen participants in the TR group and two participants in the DD group had slow drifts in their data.
This made the manual artifact rejection difficult.
Therefore, their data was filtered from 0.5 to 30 Hz instead.
This did not influence their ITC results at the frequencies of interest.
Each block then consisted of 450 syllables (150 words), which corresponds to 2.25 minutes of exposure per block.
This enabled us to perform statistical analyses on a combined sample of our data with their DD group (section 2.5.2).

In order to additionally perform an even more fine-grained time course analysis, we followed the methodology of Moreau et al. (2022) using a sliding window to map learning trajectories during the listening task.

text.text: We created epoch bundles each containing 5 epochs, with each bundle shifted by one epoch (e.g., epochs 1-5, 2-6, 3-7, etc.).
This resulted in 54 seconds of exposure per bundle and between 50 and 70 bundles per participant.

We computed the Spearman-Brown corrected split-half reliability for ITCword in the fine-grained time course analysis, splitting odd and even bundle numbers in the structured condition, as well as computing a more conservative split-half reliability using random splits with the splitHalf function from the package psych (Revelle, 2026; see RStudio supplement).
This resulted in a very high split-half reliability of .95 for ITCword during exposure to the structured language condition in the even/odd split.
For the random splits, the reliability was estimated at .78 (95%CI = [.67, .86]; see RStudio supplement).
From the bundle analysis, we extracted the maximal ITCword (maxITCword) per participant; the highest ITCword obtained during exposure to the structured language condition.
This was the dependent variable for analyses predicting individual differences in SL.

We previously took this approach in van der Wulp et al. ( 2025 and 2026a), as we observed in van der Wulp et al. (2025) that aggregated and composite measures such as the mean ITCword over exposure are not as sensitive to individual variation in behavioral SL outcomes as the maxITCword (see also the JASP supplement for the same brain-behavior correlation results with the current data).
text.formatted: We previously took this approach in van der Wulp et al. ( <ref type="formula">2025 and 2026a</ref>), as we observed in van der Wulp et al. (2025) that aggregated and composite measures such as the mean ITCword over exposure are not as sensitive to individual variation in behavioral SL outcomes as the maxITCword (see also the JASP supplement for the same brain-behavior correlation results with the current data).

text.text: The maxITCword reflects the participants' peak neural entrainment to the TP structure, and the timepoint at which this peak occurs can differ per individual.

Therefore, we hypothesize that maxITCword entails participants' maximum sensitivity to the TP structure during learning, which may be a more sensitive neural marker of SL than an aggregated measure such as the mean ITCword across exposure (van der Wulp et al., 2025).
During the rating task, participants rated the items on a four-point scale from unfamiliar (1) to familiar (4).

>Statistical analyses
text.formatted: <head n="2.5." >Statistical analyses</head>

text.text: For our statistical analyses, we followed a Bayesian methodology.
Bayesian statistical analyses take a different approach to hypothesis testing than frequentist methods.

Whereas frequentist significance testing informs us about the likelihood of the observed data under the null hypothesis (H0), Bayesian hypothesis testing allows us to estimate how plausible our alternative hypothesis (H1) is given the data collected.
The Bayes Factor (BF) is calculated as follows (Jeffreys, 1961):
text.formatted: The Bayes Factor (BF) is calculated as follows <ref type="bibr">(Jeffreys, 1961)</ref>:

text.text: The BF10 depicted above quantifies support for H1 over H0.
This is done by computing the ratio of the marginal likelihoods of H1 and H0.
The marginal likelihood of H1 is 𝑝(𝐷|H1); the likelihood of the data D given hypothesis H1.
Likewise, the marginal likelihood of H0 is 𝑝(𝐷|H0) (Nicenboim & Vasishth, 2016).
text.formatted: Likewise, the marginal likelihood of H0 is 𝑝(𝐷|H0) <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Nicenboim & Vasishth, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The subscript 10 indicates that the BF10 expresses the support for H1 compared to H0, whereas a BF01 expresses the support for H0 versus H1.
In that case, the marginal likelihoods would take opposite positions in the equation above.
To compute the marginal likelihoods of H1 and H0, we fitted Bayesian statistical models to the data that represent H1 and H0, which are then compared to retrieve the BF10.
These statistical models incorporate prior knowledge.
The prior knowledge can come from a previous experiment, meta-analysis, or expert judgements.
The aim is to include as much prior information into the models as possible, instead of starting the analysis of each dataset as if we know nothing about the topic at all.
The prior knowledge is formalized as a probability density function (e.g., a normal distribution, or a Cauchy distribution, etc.
The hyperparameters of this prior distribution, such as the mean and SD, can be taken from effect sizes of previous research.
In our case, the previous research resembling our current study the most is Zhang et al. (2021; discussed in section 1.2).
In our preregistration (van der Wulp et al., 2024) we reported our re-analysis of their data in order to estimate the size of their effects using Linear Mixed Models.

These obtained estimates of the effects of interest were subsequently used as a starting point to determine the hyperparameters of the prior distributions for our statistical models regarding the EEG data.
In the following sections describing all analyses, we elaborate on each prior distribution used.
In cases where no prior information was available, we used the package Bain (BAyesian INformative hypothesis evaluation; Gu et al., 2023; Hoijtink, Mulder, et al., 2019).
text.formatted: In cases where no prior information was available, we used the package Bain (BAyesian INformative hypothesis evaluation; <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Gu et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Hoijtink, Mulder, et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Bain computes the approximate adjusted fractional BF by comparing informative hypotheses.
These informative hypotheses can be comparisons between, for instance, group means or regression coefficients.
Bain does not rely on user-specified prior information, but instead uses a fraction of the information in the data to specify the variance of the prior distribution.

Moreover, in the case of unequal group sizes, Bain implements the multiple-population approximate adjusted fractional Bayes Factor, which was shown to be unaffected by the differences in datapoints per group (Hoijtink, Gu, et al., 2019).

text.text: We added linear, quadratic, and cubic effects per group and language condition combination (e.g., TR group linear effect in the structured condition).

This helped us to avoid forcing the model to fit, for example, a quadratic effect for all language conditions, including the random language condition, when only the structured language condition might contain a quadratic component.
We analyzed the time trends based on the urevents (the syllable number at the start of each epoch bundle, ranging from 0 to 2700) in the EEG data.
We used ur-events instead of the epoch bundle number, because our manual artifact rejection method yielded variations in the number of epoch bundles per participant and condition.
The data could have been rejected at any moment in the EEG file.

As a result, epoch bundle x for participant A could be at a different time point than epoch bundle x for participant B. The ur-events were the same at each time point for each participant, as these were not altered during artifact removal.
We standardized the time trend components by dividing the centered variables by their standard deviation, to avoid the confound that the time trends were on very different scales.
All models were fitted by sampling the posteriors in four chains of 10,000 iterations each, of which 2,000 belonged to the warming-up phase.
To assess model convergence, we visually inspected the chains, verified that there were no divergent transitions, and that the Rhat values (the between-to-within-chain variances) were close to one.
We also ensured that the effective sample size (ESS) was more than 10% of the post-warmup samples (i.e., 800 in our case), following (Nicenboim et al., 2020).

We compared the groups on their SL outcomes using three variables indexing SL ability: (1) the maxITCword, entailing the highest (maximal) ITCword per participant obtained from the bundle analysis of the EEG data in the structured language condition; (2) the familiarity rating score from the rating task; and (3) the RT score from the TDT.

We predicted, in line with earlier studies comparing SL between DD and TR groups (e.g., Zhang et al., 2021) -that the SL outcome scores would be lower on average in the DD group compared to the TR group.

text.text: We built a multiple group regression modelfoot_1 in Lavaan (Rosseel, 2012) using RStudio (Posit team, 2024) and R (R Core Team, 2024).
text.formatted: We built a multiple group regression model<ref type="foot" target="#foot_1">foot_1</ref> in Lavaan <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">(Rosseel, 2012)</ref> using RStudio (Posit team, 2024) and R (R Core Team, 2024).

text.text: We compared whether the scores on the tasks in the model were lower in the DD group compared to the TR group using Bain (Gu et al., 2023; Hoijtink, Mulder, et al., 2019).
text.formatted: We compared whether the scores on the tasks in the model were lower in the DD group compared to the TR group using Bain <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Gu et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Hoijtink, Mulder, et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: After the analyses in Bain, we conducted sensitivity analyses by increasing the fractions as described in section 2.5.3.
Based on the previous literature regarding SL and RA in DD (section 1.3.2), we predicted that the DD group would show poorer performance on the SSS task, CA-BAT, Gold-MSI, and PROMS.
Furthermore, we predicted that participants with DD would have lower scores on the Digit Span (WM; section 1.3.1) and PPVT (vocabulary).
This yielded the following hypotheses:
In Lavaan, we operationalized this by recoding the DD group as 1 and the TR group as 0.
Then, we created a new dummy variable, which represents the difference DD -TR.
If the DD group obtained a lower score on a certain task than the TR group, this variable would be negative.
After that, we specified a model where the difference variable was regressed on all tasks.

With Bain, we then evaluated the following hypotheses, with all tasks evaluated together to increase statistical power: • H0: [TASKS] ~ Group difference = 0 -the regression coefficients of the group difference DD-TR for the tasks are all not different from 0.
• H1: [TASKS] ~ Group difference < 0 -the regression coefficients of the group difference DD-TR for the tasks are smaller than 0, indicating that the DD group obtained lower scores than the TR group.
text.formatted: • H1: [TASKS] ~ Group difference < 0 -the regression coefficients of the group difference DD-TR for the tasks are smaller than 0, indicating that the DD group obtained lower scores than the TR group.

text.text: After comparing the group means on the tasks measuring RA, WM, and vocabulary, we compared the groups on the magnitude of the relationships (i.e., the regression coefficients) between these tasks and the maxITCword.
We again built a multiple group regression model in Lavaan (Rosseel, 2012) with the maxITCword as the dependent variable and the tasks for individual differences as predictors.
text.formatted: We again built a multiple group regression model in Lavaan <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">(Rosseel, 2012)</ref> with the maxITCword as the dependent variable and the tasks for individual differences as predictors.

text.text: We then compared group differences regarding the regression coefficients from the model using Bain (Gu et al., 2023; Hoijtink, Mulder, et al., 2019), testing the following hypothesis: • H1: maxITCword~[TASK]DD = maxITCword~[TASK]TR -the regression coefficients between maxITCword and the tasks do not differ between the groups This hypothesis was then compared to the unconstrained hypothesis Hu, which represents "not H1" (Hoijtink, Mulder, et al., 2019).
text.formatted: We then compared group differences regarding the regression coefficients from the model using Bain <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Gu et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Hoijtink, Mulder, et al., 2019)</ref>, testing the following hypothesis: • H1: maxITCword~[TASK]DD = maxITCword~[TASK]TR -the regression coefficients between maxITCword and the tasks do not differ between the groups This hypothesis was then compared to the unconstrained hypothesis Hu, which represents "not H1" <ref type="bibr">(Hoijtink, Mulder, et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In other words, we tested whether the regression coefficients for all tasks on the maxITCword were the same for both groups or not.

text.text: One participant in the TR group had missing data for the CA-BAT, PROMS, SSS task, Digit Span, and PPVT.
In addition, SSS data of three TR participants were excluded due to technical issues which made score calculation technically impossible.
Furthermore, TDT data of one participant in the TR group was excluded because they detected 26.3% of targets, which was below the preregistered 50% threshold (van der Wulp et al., 2024).
