>EEG results
text.formatted: <head n="3.2." >EEG results</head>

text.text: We performed two analyses on the EEG data divided over six blocks of exposure: one analysis exclusively on our newly collected data, and one with the DD sample from Zhang et al. (2021) added to our data to increase statistical power.
text.formatted: We performed two analyses on the EEG data divided over six blocks of exposure: one analysis exclusively on our newly collected data, and one with the DD sample from <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">Zhang et al. (2021)</ref> added to our data to increase statistical power.

text.text: For both analyses, the best model included only a positive effect of condition.

Adding the factor group and time trends per group and condition did not improve the model's fit to the data (see the Supplementary Materials and RStudio supplements for the details on these analyses).
Therefore, we focus the discussion of our results on the more fine-grained time-course analysis reported in the following section.
We analyzed the ITCword as a function of exposure in both conditions using the sliding-window overlapping epoch bundle approach.
Each participant had between 50 and 70 epoch bundles, yielding more statistical power than the block analyses (section 3.2.1).
Here, we report the model building procedure and results from the best model.
For the full model building results including sensitivity analyses, see Appendix A.1.
We have additionally repeated this analysis while excluding the four participants with comorbid ADHD.
This did not alter the results presented below.
The model building results and sensitivity analyses for this sample are reported in Appendix A.2.
The null model included a random intercept for participant.
Language condition (structured/random) added as a fixed factor highly improved the model's fit (BF10 (0, 0.135) > 1000).
text.formatted: Language condition (structured/random) added as a fixed factor highly improved the model's fit (BF10 (0, 0.135) > 1000).

text.text: Adding language condition as a random slope per participant also drastically improved the model (BF10 (1) > 1000), but subsequent models including condition, group, and time trends combined with these random slopes did not converge.
text.formatted: Adding language condition as a random slope per participant also drastically improved the model (BF10 (1) > 1000), but subsequent models including condition, group, and time trends combined with these random slopes did not converge.

text.text: Therefore, we initially left the random slopes for language condition out of the model and added them later again to the best model.
Group (DD/TR) did not improve the model's fit to the data (BF10 (0, 0.2) = 0.04).
However, because investigating group differences was a critical part of the current study, we retained group in the model.
We also found evidence for no interaction of language condition and group (BF10 (0, 0.2) = 0.05), which was then not retained in the model.

In the random condition, the quadratic time trend for the TR group improved the model with a negative quadratic effect (BF10 (0, 0.2) = 5.04), which was not robust against increasing the prior (Appendix A.1).
None of the other time trends in the random condition improved the model for either group.

Thus, the best model at this stage of the analysis included a random intercept for participant, fixed effects of condition and group, as well as a linear time trend for the TR group, a quadratic time trend (positive) for the DD group in the structured condition, and a negative quadratic time trend for the TR group in the random condition.
Then, we continued to estimate the best model for our data.
As the fixed factor group had not received evidence that it improved the model, we first continued by removing the fixed effect of group, which improved the model (BF10 (0, 0.2) = 16.42).
We subsequently added the random slopes for condition per participant back into the model, which also improved the model's fit (BF10 (0, 0.2) > 1000).
text.formatted: We subsequently added the random slopes for condition per participant back into the model, which also improved the model's fit (BF10 (0, 0.2) > 1000).

text.text: We re-estimated the BFs for each time trend and the effect of condition in the model now that the model included random slopes.

Removing the quadratic time trend for the TR group in the random condition improved the model's fit now that the random slopes were included, indicated by increasing evidence as the prior increased (BF10 (0, 0.2) = 1.38; BF10 (0, 0.5) = 3.64; BF10 (0, 1) = 7.66).

Removing the linear and quadratic time trends in the structured condition for the TR and DD groups respectively did not improve the model's fit and they were retained (linear TR: BF10 (0, 0.2) = 0.00, quadratic DD: BF10 (0, 0.2) = 0.02).
Removing the fixed effect of language condition resulted in robust anecdotal evidence that removing it would improve the model (BF10 (0, 0.2) = 2.85).
This is probably due to the time trend analysis, which estimated trends per condition.

However, as we initially received strong evidence that condition improved the model, the difference in model posterior predictive results was very small (see Figure B1 in Appendix B), and this result showed BF10 < 3, we decided to retain condition as a fixed factor in the final model.
text.formatted: However, as we initially received strong evidence that condition improved the model, the difference in model posterior predictive results was very small (see Figure <ref type="figure">B1</ref> in Appendix B), and this result showed BF10 < 3, we decided to retain condition as a fixed factor in the final model.

text.text: Finally, due to the large age range in the current study, we included age in the best model.
This resulted in strong evidence that age did not affect the results presented above (BF10 (0, 0.2) = 0.002).

The final model included an effect of language condition (βstructured compared to random = 0.01, SD = 0.005, 95% CrI [0.001, 0.02]), indicating overall stronger entrainment to the word frequency in the structured condition for both groups.

The model also included a linear effect in the structured condition for the TR group (β = 0.01, SD = 0.002, 95% CrI [0.006, 0.01]), describing the increase in word-level entrainment as the exposure time increased.

Finally, the model included a quadratic effect in the structured condition for the DD group (β = 0.02, SD = 0.004, 95% CrI [0.009, 0.03]), modelling their learning curve in entrainment, initially decreasing, and then increasing in parallel with the TR group (cf.
Figure 4).

text.text: Therefore, we decided to further explore individual differences in SL (represented by the maxITCword) in both groups combined as one population.
We conducted a Bayesian regression analysis in JASP with Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA; van den Bergh et al., 2021; van der Wulp et al., 2026b).
text.formatted: We conducted a Bayesian regression analysis in JASP with Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA; <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">van den Bergh et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b111">van der Wulp et al., 2026b)</ref>.

text.text: BMA provides parameter estimates for each predictor after considering all possible models with all possible combinations of the predictors.
In other words, BMA selects the best model with the predictors that best fit the data.
We followed the methodology for BMA as described in the tutorial by van den Bergh et al. (2021).
text.formatted: We followed the methodology for BMA as described in the tutorial by <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">van den Bergh et al. (2021)</ref>.

text.text: The dependent variable of our regression models was the maxITCword.
Predictors were the scores on the tasks for individual differences (SSS PLV, Gold-MSI, CA-BAT, PROMS, Digit Span, and PPVT).

We determined which model was the best model, and what the relative contribution of each predictor was given the data, by looking at the posterior inclusion probabilities of the predictors (van den Bergh et al., 2021).
text.formatted: We determined which model was the best model, and what the relative contribution of each predictor was given the data, by looking at the posterior inclusion probabilities of the predictors <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">(van den Bergh et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: For BMA, two priors need to be specified.
The first prior is the model prior, representing the prior belief that some models are more probable than others.
We considered all models to be equally probable, and therefore adhered to the neutral choice of the uniform distribution (van den Bergh et al., 2021).
text.formatted: We considered all models to be equally probable, and therefore adhered to the neutral choice of the uniform distribution <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">(van den Bergh et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The second prior represents the prior distribution for the regression coefficients: the regression prior.
We chose the default Jeffreys-Zellner-Siouw (JZS) prior.
This is a multivariate Cauchy distribution on the beta coefficients of the model.
The scale determining the width of the JZS prior is defined by r.
We adhered to the default choice in JASP: 𝑟 = √ 18 = 0.354.
This is a "medium" scale for the JZS prior (van den Bergh et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This is a "medium" scale for the JZS prior <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">(van den Bergh et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Sensitivity analyses encompassed varying both the model and regression priors to determine the robustness of the outcomes.
Regarding the model prior, robustness was determined with a beta-binominal model prior, adhering to the default settings α = β = 1 (following van den Bergh et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Regarding the model prior, robustness was determined with a beta-binominal model prior, adhering to the default settings α = β = 1 (following <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">van den Bergh et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This prior assigns equal probability to models with the same number of predictors.

The best model included the Digit Span and SSS PLV as predictors and obtained an R² of 0.08, indicating that this model accounts for 8% of the variance in maxITCword.
The predictors Digit Span and SSS PLV received anecdotal Bayes Factors in the model averaged posterior summary, and their effects were very small (Table 5).
text.formatted: The predictors Digit Span and SSS PLV received anecdotal Bayes Factors in the model averaged posterior summary, and their effects were very small (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">5</ref>).

text.text: Sensitivity analyses by increasing the regression prior to wide and ultrawide did not alter these results (see JASP supplement).

However, the sensitivity analysis concerning the model prior (using the beta binomial prior instead of the uniform prior) yielded the BMA analysis to favor the null model over all other possible models.
Also, when we excluded the four participants with comorbid ADHD, or used the averaged ITCword as the dependent variable, the null model became the best model in all analyses (see JASP supplement).

Thus, it seems that WM and sensorimotor synchronization comprise positive yet very small contributions to SL in our combined sample, as represented by the maxITCword, leaving most of the variance unexplained.

The aim of the current study was to investigate individual differences in Statistical Learning (SL) for speech segmentation in individuals with Developmental Dyslexia (DD), compared to Typical Readers (TR), as well as investigating individual differences in SL within these populations.
Specifically, we hypothesized correlations between Working Memory (WM) and musical Rhythmic Ability (RA) to SL in both groups.
We predicted that regardless of diagnosis, RA and WM are positively related to SL.
Furthermore, we explored whether SL ability related positively to a larger vocabulary size.

We investigated (1) whether the DD group showed poorer SL ability, both behaviorally and neurally, compared to the TR group; (2) whether adults with DD obtained lower scores on tasks measuring RA, WM, and vocabulary size, compared to the TR group; and; (3) whether interindividual variations in RA, WM capacity and vocabulary size similarly related to individual differences in SL abilities in individuals with DD compared to typical readers.

As we did not find differences in on-line SL ability between the groups, as well as no differences in the relations between RA, WM, vocabulary, and their contributions to SL, we additionally explored individual differences in SL by combining both groups into one population.
>No neural evidence for impaired statistical learning in Developmental
text.formatted: <head n="4.1." >No neural evidence for impaired statistical learning in Developmental</head>

text.text: We found Bayesian statistical evidence supporting the null hypothesis that there were no differences in neural measures of SL between the DD and TR groups.
During the listening task, both groups successfully segmented the structured speech stream based on the transitional probabilities (TPs).

This was indicated for both groups by their neural entrainment to the word frequency (ITCword) in the structured language condition, and absence of such entrainment in the random (unstructured) condition.

Furthermore, we derived the maximal ITCword for each participant, and again found statistical evidence that the DD and TR groups reached similar maximal neural entrainment to the word frequency in the structured language condition.
These results indicate that our DD and TR groups did not differ in SL as indicated by neural entrainment.
The groups did seem to show slightly different learning curves over time in the structured language condition, as initial word-level entrainment in the DD group was unexpectedly high (cf.
Figure 4).
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">4</ref>).

text.text: This led to a positive quadratic learning curve (initial decrease Mean and SD represent the posterior means and standard deviations of the predictor after model averaging.

followed by an increase of entrainment) being the best-fitting time trend for the DD group, whereas the TR group's learning curve was best fitted with a positive linear time trend.
These results could be due to differences in group sizes, as the DD group was significantly smaller than the TR group, which increases variance in the time trend estimations for the DD group.
Further research with a larger DD group needs to be conducted to shed light on this issue.

Interestingly, both groups did show highly similar neural entrainment to the word frequency towards the end of exposure: both groups showed a relatively late increase in ITCword in the structured language condition (see also van der Wulp et al., 2025).

text.text: As previously touched upon in van der Wulp et al. (2025), this could be due to properties of the stimuli used in the current project.
text.formatted: As previously touched upon in van der <ref type="bibr" target="#b112">Wulp et al. (2025)</ref>, this could be due to properties of the stimuli used in the current project.

text.text: Specifically, we used co-articulated speech streams instead of separately recorded syllables, and avoided using syllables that were existing single-syllabic words or frequent forms in Dutch.
This was not controlled for in the stimuli used by Zhang et al. (2021) and related previous work (e.g., Batterink & Paller, 2017; Saffran, Aslin et al., 1996).

text.text: The relatively infrequently occurring syllables in Dutch used in the current study could have influenced the time-course of neural entrainment in both groups, as they may have been less familiar to the participants.
In contrast to the neural entrainment results, evidence from the post-exposure behavioral tasks used to measure SL outcomes -the rating task and the TDT -was less clear.
The results indicated lower mean scores for the DD group than for the TR group, especially in the TDT.
However, the evidence was statistically anecdotal and only became stronger when a larger portion of the variance in the sample was used to estimate the prior in the sensitivity analysis (Table 2).
text.formatted: However, the evidence was statistically anecdotal and only became stronger when a larger portion of the variance in the sample was used to estimate the prior in the sensitivity analysis (Table <ref type="table">2</ref>).

text.text: Moreover, the DD group showed variance overlapping with the TR group (Figure 5), which points to individual variability in both samples.
text.formatted: Moreover, the DD group showed variance overlapping with the TR group (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_8">5</ref>), which points to individual variability in both samples.

text.text: As the behavioral tasks were completed after the familiarization phase, the scores are not only dependent on SL, but also require memory storage of the segmented words and metacognitive decision making (e.g., Bogaerts et al., 2022).
text.formatted: As the behavioral tasks were completed after the familiarization phase, the scores are not only dependent on SL, but also require memory storage of the segmented words and metacognitive decision making (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Bogaerts et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: SL can conceptually be distinguished into two components: an identification component (i.e., computing the TPs and extracting word forms from the speech stream, measured with neural entrainment) and a memorization component (i.e., transferring these word forms from short-term to long-term memory, measured in behavioral post-learning tasks; Batterink & Paller, 2017).
text.formatted: SL can conceptually be distinguished into two components: an identification component (i.e., computing the TPs and extracting word forms from the speech stream, measured with neural entrainment) and a memorization component (i.e., transferring these word forms from short-term to long-term memory, measured in behavioral post-learning tasks; <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Batterink & Paller, 2017</ref>).

text.text: An explanation for our mixed neural and behavioral results could be that the DD population has difficulties with this memory transfer process, but not with the identification component of SL.
This would agree with work by Ballan et al. (2023), which has shown poorer consolidation of acquired statistical regularities into long-term memory for individuals with DD.
text.formatted: This would agree with work by <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Ballan et al. (2023)</ref>, which has shown poorer consolidation of acquired statistical regularities into long-term memory for individuals with DD.

text.text: Further work in that direction is necessary to conclude whether or not the memorization component of SL is affected in individuals with DD.
Another explanation for the brain-behavior dissociation in our findings could be psychometric in nature.

Split-half reliability of the behavioral tasks assessing SL was not high (around .48 for both the rating task and TDT), comparable to an insufficient reliability of behavioral auditory SL tasks in the previous literature (e.g., Arnon, 2020, reported a split-half reliability of .43 in their first session with adults), whereas the reliability of the EEG data was good (.95 in an even/odd split, .78 averaged over random splits.
This supports the view that neural entrainment during exposure is a more reliable measure of SL on the individual level than post-exposure behavioral tasks.
The results of our study indicated that the DD group obtained lower scores on the tasks measuring RA, WM, and vocabulary size, when group differences for all tasks were evaluated together.

A visual inspection of these results (Figure 6) indicated that the standard deviations showed a large overlap for most tasks, while the means of the DD group on the Digit Span (measuring verbal WM) and the PPVT (measuring age-normed vocabulary size) were approximately one standard deviation below the mean of the TR group.
text.formatted: A visual inspection of these results (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">6</ref>) indicated that the standard deviations showed a large overlap for most tasks, while the means of the DD group on the Digit Span (measuring verbal WM) and the PPVT (measuring age-normed vocabulary size) were approximately one standard deviation below the mean of the TR group.

text.text: This suggests that the effect may be primarily driven by the scores on the Digit Span and PPVT, rather than scores on tasks measuring RA or musicality.

Our results do not indicate clear rhythmic impairments in DD, contrasting with findings reported in the literature consisting of both behavioral (e.g., Bégel et al., 2022; Boll-Avetisyan et al., 2020; Caccia & Lorusso, 2021; Flaugnacco et al., 2014; Huss et al., 2011) and neural investigations (e.g., Chang et al., 2021; Colling et al., 2017; Peter et al., 2023; Power et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Our results do not indicate clear rhythmic impairments in DD, contrasting with findings reported in the literature consisting of both behavioral (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Bégel et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Boll-Avetisyan et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Caccia & Lorusso, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Flaugnacco et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Huss et al., 2011)</ref> and neural investigations (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Chang et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Colling et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Peter et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Power et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: However, this discrepancy might be dependent on other factors, such as differences in the tasks and age groups that were assessed in these previous studies.
To our knowledge, only Bégel et al. (2022) employed a type of beat alignment task -similar to our CA-BAT -to investigate DD and TR group differences.
text.formatted: To our knowledge, only <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Bégel et al. (2022)</ref> employed a type of beat alignment task -similar to our CA-BAT -to investigate DD and TR group differences.

text.text: However, their task was not identical to the one we used, and their investigation focused on children.
We were unable to find publications comparing DD and TR groups on the rhythm and accent sub-tests of the PROMS.
In general, differences between tasks used to measure RA could contribute to differences between studies investigating RA.

For instance, in our previous publication involving part of the TR group from the current study (van der Wulp et al., 2025), we found that the scores on the PROMS (Zentner & Strauss, 2017) and CA-BAT (Harrison & Müllensiefen, 2018b , 2018a) correlated positively only after we included more than 90 participants, showing inconclusive evidence with smaller samples.
text.formatted: For instance, in our previous publication involving part of the TR group from the current study <ref type="bibr" target="#b112">(van der Wulp et al., 2025)</ref>, we found that the scores on the PROMS <ref type="bibr" target="#b119">(Zentner & Strauss, 2017)</ref> and CA-BAT <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Harrison & Müllensiefen, 2018b</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2018a)</ref> correlated positively only after we included more than 90 participants, showing inconclusive evidence with smaller samples.

text.text: These tasks both aim to measure RA, but do so in quite different ways (i.e., comparing rhythmic sequences in the PROMS versus assessing beat alignment of a metronome to naturalistic music in the CA-BAT).
RA is also often measured as the accuracy of sensorimotor synchronization, most commonly through finger-tapping tasks (e.g., Bégel et al., 2022).
text.formatted: RA is also often measured as the accuracy of sensorimotor synchronization, most commonly through finger-tapping tasks (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Bégel et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: We employed the SSS task (Assaneo et al., 2019) as a sensorimotor synchronization task, which correlated highly with the CA-BAT and the Gold-MSI but not with the PROMS in the typical population (van der Wulp et al., 2025).
text.formatted: We employed the SSS task <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Assaneo et al., 2019)</ref> as a sensorimotor synchronization task, which correlated highly with the CA-BAT and the Gold-MSI but not with the PROMS in the typical population <ref type="bibr" target="#b112">(van der Wulp et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, differences in task demands contribute to differing findings regarding (impaired) RA in diverse groups.

Theoretical frameworks positing that individuals with DD have impaired RA argue that this is related to inefficient neural entrainment to auditory rhythmic stimuli (e.g., PRISM; Fiveash et al., 2021; Temporal Sampling Framework; Goswami, 2011; Atypical Rhythm Risk Hypothesis; Ladányi et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Theoretical frameworks positing that individuals with DD have impaired RA argue that this is related to inefficient neural entrainment to auditory rhythmic stimuli (e.g., PRISM; <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Fiveash et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Temporal Sampling Framework;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Goswami, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Atypical Rhythm Risk Hypothesis;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Ladányi et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: These frameworks make predictions on the neural level, while we employed behavioral tasks as a proxy for RA.
Neural processing of rhythms may not necessarily translate to behavioral tasks measuring RA such as the ones administered in the current study.
Future work could further investigate how neural processing of auditory rhythms is related to behavioral tasks measuring RA in populations with and without DD.

We found indications for group differences in WM capacity, with the DD group showing a smaller WM span as indicated by scores on the Digit Span being almost one standard deviation lower than in the TR group (Figure 6).
text.formatted: We found indications for group differences in WM capacity, with the DD group showing a smaller WM span as indicated by scores on the Digit Span being almost one standard deviation lower than in the TR group (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">6</ref>).

text.text: This result is in line with our predictions and the previous literature reporting that individuals with DD have smaller phonological WM spans persisting into adulthood (Gabay et al., 2015; Smith-Spark & Fisk, 2007).
text.formatted: This result is in line with our predictions and the previous literature reporting that individuals with DD have smaller phonological WM spans persisting into adulthood <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Gabay et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">Smith-Spark & Fisk, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Still, similar to Gray et al. (2019), our DD group showed large individual variability in their Digit Span scores, with overlap in the ranges of scores between the DD and TR groups.
text.formatted: Still, similar to <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Gray et al. (2019)</ref>, our DD group showed large individual variability in their Digit Span scores, with overlap in the ranges of scores between the DD and TR groups.

text.text: Based on these results, we cannot say that WM impairments are universal in the adult population diagnosed with DD.
Future studies may want to focus on investigating individual differences in WM components within an adult group diagnosed with DD, similar to previous work with children by Gray et al. (2019).
text.formatted: Future studies may want to focus on investigating individual differences in WM components within an adult group diagnosed with DD, similar to previous work with children by <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Gray et al. (2019)</ref>.

text.text: The DD participants' receptive vocabulary sizes were smaller than those of the TR participants, as indicated by their PPVT scores, which were around one standard deviation below the TR group's mean.
This is in line with previous research showing that adults who were diagnosed with DD in childhood have smaller vocabularies than their typically reading peers (e.g., Ransby & Lee Swanson, 2003).
text.formatted: This is in line with previous research showing that adults who were diagnosed with DD in childhood have smaller vocabularies than their typically reading peers (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Ransby & Lee Swanson, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: However, again, there was large individual variability within the DD group and overlap between the scores of the DD and TR groups.
An average smaller vocabulary in DD may be due to less print exposure, as this is positively related to vocabulary size (e.g., Misyak & Christiansen, 2012; Suk, 2017).
text.formatted: An average smaller vocabulary in DD may be due to less print exposure, as this is positively related to vocabulary size (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Misyak & Christiansen, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">Suk, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Future studies may therefore want to incorporate a measure of print exposure (e.g., reading frequency) as a covariate when investigating adult vocabulary size in DD.

We explored whether the groups differed in their regression coefficients (i.e., steepness of the linear relation between predictor and dependent variable) between the tasks measuring individual differences and the neural measure of SL (maximal ITCword in the structured condition).
Our hypothesis was that a relation between RA or WM and SL, if found, would be the same for both groups, which predicts that the coefficients would not differ between the groups.
In that case, difficulties with SL in the DD group could be (partially) explained by impairments in RA or WM.
Indeed, we found statistical evidence for equality of the regression coefficients.

However, this result became inconclusive in our sensitivity analysis. Hoijtink, Mulder, et al. (2019) argue that robust evidence is needed before any hypothesis is preferred over the null hypothesis specifying that there are no group differences.
text.formatted: However, this result became inconclusive in our sensitivity analysis. <ref type="bibr">Hoijtink, Mulder, et al. (2019)</ref> argue that robust evidence is needed before any hypothesis is preferred over the null hypothesis specifying that there are no group differences.

text.text: In our case, we cannot conclude that we found statistical evidence for differences regarding the regression coefficients between the groups, but we can also not conclude that there are no differences at all.
Upon visual inspection of the coefficients per group (Figure 7), we established that the credible intervals showed overlap in most cases.
text.formatted: Upon visual inspection of the coefficients per group (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_11">7</ref>), we established that the credible intervals showed overlap in most cases.

text.text: This points to individual variability -rather than a group distinction -and likely is the reason we found inconclusive evidence for the hypothesis that the coefficients did not differ between the groups.

Our group comparisons suggest that the DD group on average reached similar maximal sensitivity to the TP-structure (i.e., the identification component of SL) to segment the speech stream in the structured language condition, and that the groups did not differ regarding the relations between individual difference measures and SL.
Therefore, we exploratively investigated individual differences in SL in the combined sample including all participants from both groups together as one population (N = 143).

The best model predicting individual differences in the maximal ITCword initially included very small positive contributions to SL from the Digit Span and SSS PLV, but the null model became the best model in the sensitivity analyses.
Taken together, it seems that WM and sensorimotor synchronization have small positive effects on SL (as indicated by the maximal neural entrainment to the word frequency) in our combined sample.
Overall, our results suggest that the identification component of SL is largely independent from other cognitive abilities such as RA and WM in both typical readers and individuals with DD.
This is in line with the account that SL ability is independent of general cognitive abilities such as general intelligence (Siegelman & Frost, 2015).
text.formatted: This is in line with the account that SL ability is independent of general cognitive abilities such as general intelligence <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">(Siegelman & Frost, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: We extended this line of research on possible cognitive factors interacting with SL to musical and rhythmic abilities.
Furthermore, we assessed SL not only with behavioral tasks, but also with neural measurements able to assess the identification component of SL during learning.
In contrast, our measurements of RA relied on behavioral tasks, which may be less 'pure' than, for instance, neural entrainment to rhythmic stimuli.
We recommend that future studies employ more direct (neural) outcome measures for constructs hypothesized to interact with SL.
Studies investigating neurodevelopmental disorders have frequently focused on group comparisons, classifying the group with a certain diagnosis as 'one kind of individual.'
The current study emphasized that individual variability is a crucial factor for consideration when investigating cognitive processes in neurodiverse populations compared to their neurotypical peers.
As discussed by Mirman (2014, Chapter 7), individual differences are highly valuable when investigating a cognitive process such as SL.
They are not just random variance but constrain a theory of a cognitive system by describing how the system's behavior can vary.
A good theoretical account for SL should explain individual variation in SL in the typical population as well as in atypical populations.

It could then very well be that individuals with a certain diagnosis are often outperformed by their neurotypical peers, but our results do not indicate that this is consistently the case for SL in individuals diagnosed with DD.
Our neural entrainment results suggest that SL for speech segmentation is not impaired in the population diagnosed with DD, but the behavioral post-exposure evidence is less clear.

The current study was limited in its sample of participants with DD, by relying on self-reported diagnosis status, and diagnostic heterogeneity in moment of diagnosis or (current) symptom severity may have contributed to these results.
Future studies investigating SL in DD are therefore advised to take inventory of the full diagnostic profile of individuals with DD, complemented with an individual differences approach.
This way, future studies can shed light on which factors could contribute to individual differences in SL within the DD population.
This can be done by, for example, assessing print exposure, phonological awareness, and reading performance per participant.
For instance, phonological awareness was previously found to relate to SL ability in DD (Zhang et al., 2021).
text.formatted: For instance, phonological awareness was previously found to relate to SL ability in DD <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">(Zhang et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Due to the length of the experimental session in the current study (approximately two hours), we did not include tasks measuring phonological awareness or additional reading or writing tasks.
Since RA and general language abilities have been found to correlate in several studies, it is possible that factors such as phonological awareness can be predicted by RA.
In turn, phonological awareness may then predict individual differences in SL.

This is in line with the 'noisy chain' hypothesis put forward by Schmalz et al. (2021), stating that each intermediary step between a proposed underlying mechanism and the end-state of an ability dilutes the correlation coefficient between the low-level deficit and the end-state outcome.
text.formatted: This is in line with the 'noisy chain' hypothesis put forward by <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">Schmalz et al. (2021)</ref>, stating that each intermediary step between a proposed underlying mechanism and the end-state of an ability dilutes the correlation coefficient between the low-level deficit and the end-state outcome.

text.text: Future studies may want to investigate mediations and moderations with such intermediary factors influencing relations between cognitive constructs such as RA or WM and SL in a variety of populations.
We obtained statistical evidence for SL for speech segmentation in both DD and TR groups, with similar word-form learning during exposure in the EEG data.
In the behavioral tasks assessing SL outcomes after the learning phase, the DD group obtained lower scores than the TR group, but the Bayes Factors pertaining to these differences were anecdotal.
The DD group also obtained lower scores on tasks measuring individual differences in RA, WM, and vocabulary size, compared to the TR group.
Visual inspection of these results suggested that this difference was primarily driven by the tasks measuring WM and vocabulary, rather than RA.

Comparison of regression coefficients between a neural measure of SL ability and the tasks measuring individual differences did not provide conclusive evidence for differences between the groups in how these tasks related to SL.
Finally, we exploratively investigated individual differences in SL by combining both groups into one sample.
This revealed anecdotal evidence that individual differences in SL are weakly correlated with WM and sensorimotor synchronization, which, however, was not robust in our sensitivity analyses.
Our results emphasize the importance of an individual differences approach, moving beyond group comparisons alone.

text.text: In all analyses, we computed the ITCs for the 20 frontocentral electrodes previously selected byMoreau et  al.

(2022)3 . of epochs Φ(f, i) = Phase at frequency f and trial iThe ITC to the word frequency (ITCword) and ITC to the syllable frequency (ITCsyllable) were calculated as the mean for each participant over the entire exposure period, as well as over the time-course of exposure in both structured and random language conditions.
The stimuli were presented to the participants in three blocks of 4.5 minutes each (13.5 minutes per condition; see section 2.3.1), where each block consisted of 900 syllables (300 words).
FollowingZhang et al. (2021), we divided the data into six blocks for a more fine-grained time-course analysis.
Results of the time trend analyses indicated that the linear time trend in the structured condition for the TR group improved the model (BF10 (0, 0.2) > 1000).
text.formatted: Results of the time trend analyses indicated that the linear time trend in the structured condition for the TR group improved the model (BF10 (0, 0.2) > 1000).

text.text: The quadratic and cubic time trends did not (BF10 (0, 0.2) = 0.18, and BF10 (0, 0.2) = 0.02, respectively).
In contrast, the linear time trend in the structured language condition did not improve the model for the DD group (BF10 (0, 0.2) = 0.02).
The evidence that the quadratic time trend for the DD group improved the model was anecdotal (BF10 (0, 0.2) = 2.33), and not robust against increasing the prior (see Appendix A.1).
The cubic time trend also did not improve the model for the DD group (BF10 (0, 0.2) = 0.01).

We retained the quadratic time trend for the DD group in the structured condition because it was the time trend that received comparatively the most evidence, as well as descriptively the most fitting (see Figure4for a plot of ITCword entrainment over time in both groups and conditions).
